messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Answer**

For a projectile (or a “car” that is launched into the air) the motion can be split into horizontal and vertical components.  
Let  

* \(v\) – initial speed (m s⁻¹)  
* \(\theta\) – launch angle measured from the horizontal (degrees)  
* \(t\) – elapsed time after launch (s)  
* \(g = 9.81\;\text{m s}^{-2}\) – acceleration due to gravity (downward)

---

### 1. Horizontal distance travelled in time \(t\)

The horizontal component of the velocity is constant:

\[
v_x = v \cos\theta
\]

Hence the horizontal displacement after time \(t\) is

\[
\boxed{\,x(t) = v \cos\theta \; t\,}
\]

If you only care about how far the car has moved horizontally, this is the answer.

---

### 2. Vertical displacement after time \(t\)

The vertical component of the velocity changes under gravity:

\[
v_y(t) = v \sin\theta - g\,t
\]

The vertical position relative to the launch point is

\[
\boxed{\,y(t) = v \sin\theta \; t \;-\; \tfrac12 g t^{2}\,}
\]

---

### 3. Total distance travelled along the trajectory

If you want the *arc length* of the path up to time \(t\) (i.e., the distance the car has actually travelled along its curved trajectory), you combine the horizontal and vertical displacements:

\[
\boxed{\,s(t) = \sqrt{\bigl(v \cos\theta \; t\bigr)^{2} \;+\;
          \bigl(v \sin\theta \; t \;-\; \tfrac12 g t^{2}\bigr)^{2}\,}}
\]

This gives the straight‑line distance from the launch point to the car’s position at time \(t\).

---

### 4. Special case: full flight range

If you’re interested in the *total horizontal range* (the distance from launch to landing), you first find the flight time \(T\) when the vertical position returns to zero:

\[
0 = v \sin\theta \; T \;-\; \tfrac12 g T^{2}
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
T = \frac{2 v \sin\theta}{g}
\]

Plugging this into the horizontal distance formula gives the classic range:

\[
\boxed{\,R = v^{2}\,\frac{\sin(2\theta)}{g}\,}
\]

---

#### Quick reference

| Quantity | Formula |
|----------|---------|
| Horizontal distance after \(t\) | \(x = v \cos\theta \; t\) |
| Vertical displacement after \(t\) | \(y = v \sin\theta \; t - \tfrac12 g t^{2}\) |
| Path length after \(t\) | \(s = \sqrt{(v \cos\theta \; t)^{2} + (v \sin\theta \; t - \tfrac12 g t^{2})^{2}}\) |
| Full range (landing) | \(R = \dfrac{v^{2}\sin(2\theta)}{g}\) |

Just plug in your numbers (remember to convert \(\theta\) to radians if you’re using a calculator that expects radians).
